title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) is a postinfectious inflammatory condition associated with COVID-19 that can affect multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurologic systems. Although rare in neonates, MIS-C in this population can present with variable and nonspecific signs, such as fever, rash, conjunctivitis, poor feeding, and gastrointestinal symptoms, which may occasionally progress to shock and multiorgan failure. The pathophysiology is believed to involve an exaggerated immune response following exposure to the virus, resulting in cytokine release, endothelial injury, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and relies on evidence of recent COVID-19 exposure, laboratory evidence of inflammation, and exclusion of other conditions such as sepsis or Kawasaki disease. Early recognition and prompt management are crucial, as timely initiation of intravenous immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and supportive care has been associated with improved survival and reduced complications.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through participation in this continuing education activity, clinicians gain a deeper understanding of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and diagnostic criteria of MIS-C in neonates. Learners enhance their competence in recognizing the diverse manifestations of MIS-C and in differentiating it from other infectious or inflammatory conditions. The course also reviews evidence-based management strategies, emphasizing appropriate use of immunomodulatory therapy, supportive care, and follow-up to monitor for long-term sequelae. Collaboration among an interprofessional healthcare team—comprising neonatal and pediatric intensivists, cardiologists, infectious disease specialists, rheumatologists, and hematologists—optimizes diagnostic accuracy, guides individualized therapy, and improves overall patient outcomes through shared expertise and coordinated care.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Introduction
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) declared a coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic in March 2020. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19 infection, which may present with acute respiratory distress syndrome, affecting individuals of all ages. In adults, COVID-19 commonly leads to acute respiratory failure. In children, COVID-19 usually has a milder clinical course and a more favorable outcome. In contrast to adults and older children, COVID-19 infection is uncommon in neonates. [1]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Introduction
content: The low incidence of COVID-19 infection in neonates is attributed to the limited availability of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors in the nasal epithelium, considered the primary point of entry for COVID-19 in the human body. However, hyperinflammatory shock and organ failure cases were reported in neonates and older children with previous COVID-19 infection and positive antibodies. Subsequently, a different disease entity associated with COVID-19 in children was described as a multisystem inflammatory syndrome related to COVID-19 (MIS-C).

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Introduction
content: The definition of MIS-C related to COVID-19 has undergone significant changes. The original Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) definition posed challenges in differentiating MIS-C from severe COVID-19, prompting revisions by the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) and the CDC. Implemented on January 1, 2023, the new criteria include notable modifications, such as removing the requirement for fever duration; the requirement of involvement of at least two organ systems, with shock added as a separate category; and specification of elevated C-reactive protein (CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL) as an inflammatory marker. The timeframe for MIS-C diagnosis was extended to up to 60 days following a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result. These revisions improve the distinction between MIS-C and other illnesses, reduce misclassification, and enhance the feasibility of implementation. [2] The updated definition eliminates respiratory, neurologic, and renal criteria and designates Kawasaki disease as an alternative diagnosis. See Image . Surveillance Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Etiology
content: Neonatal cases of COVID-19 infection are primarily due to horizontal transmission, although vertical transmission has been reported. [3] However, recent evidence suggests that vertical transmission is infrequent, possibly due to low placental expression of the canonical receptors required for viral entry. [4] Although the exact etiology of MIS-C remains speculative, it is postulated to result from a hyperinflammatory response following either symptomatic or asymptomatic COVID-19 infection, rather than direct cell injury caused by the virus. Proposed mechanisms include: Maternal COVID-19 infection and transplacental transfer of maternal antibodies. Transplacental transfer of maternal infection with subsequent endogenous production of antibodies in the neonate. Neonatal COVID-19 infection followed by a postinfectious immune response. [5]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Epidemiology
content: There is a paucity of data on the incidence of COVID-19 and MIS-C in neonates. Most neonatal MIS-C data are from case reports and case series. [6] [7] Overall, neonates appear to have a lower incidence of COVID-19 infection and MIS-C compared to older children. [8]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Epidemiology
content: According to CDC data, the overall incidence of MIS-C in 2023 was 0.11 cases per million person-months (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.10–0.14), an 80% reduction compared with April to December 2022, which reported 0.56 cases per million person-months (95% CI, 0.51–0.62). This also signifies a 98% drop from the peak incidence of 6.79 (95% CI, 6.56–7.03) observed early in the COVID-19 pandemic, between October 2020 and April 2021. [9] The decline in cases may reflect the evolution of population immunity, shaped by vaccination, prior infection, and the characteristics of the prevailing SARS-CoV-2 variants.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Pathophysiology
content: The exact pathophysiology of MIS-C is unknown, but it may occur due to an immune-mediated mechanism leading to a cytokine storm and oxidative stress. The cause of immune dysregulation and cytokine storm after COVID-19 infection in children and neonates remains unclear. However, maternal COVID-19 infection during pregnancy can impact the developing fetal immune system. Findings from case reports indicate elevated inflammatory markers and cytokine activity in fetuses of mothers with active COVID-19 infections during pregnancy. Less is known about the impact of exposure timing and whether these inflammatory responses are transient. [10]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Pathophysiology
content: Findings from placental studies of mothers exposed to COVID-19 infection during pregnancy revealed thrombotic and vascular changes, suggesting an inflammatory risk to the fetus even in the absence of an active viral infection in the fetus or neonate. [11] During maternal COVID-19 infection, protective maternal immunoglobulin (Ig)G antibodies are transferred to the fetus via the transplacental route. In some neonates, this may trigger the production of autoantibodies that bind to neutrophil and macrophage receptors, leading to a cytokine response and MIS-C development. [12] [13]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Pathophysiology
content: Depending on the timing of COVID-19 exposure in the mother, this reaction can occur prenatally or postnatally. Neonates exposed to the maternal COVID-19 infection during the antenatal period may develop an inflammatory response postnatally, developing MIS-C. Thus, MIS-C can develop due to immune-mediated multisystem injury through transplacental antibody transfer or antibodies from a neonatal COVID-19 infection. [12] [14]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- History and Physical
content: The clinical signs and symptoms of MIS-C are highly variable. Since MIS-C is a postinfectious immune sequela of COVID-19, a 2 to 6-week latency often follows COVID-19 exposure before symptom onset. Infants with a history of maternal COVID-19 exposure may present earlier due to the transmission of antibodies across the placenta. The presentation ranges from asymptomatic infection to multiorgan failure; infants may present with or without fever. Signs of inflammation and multiorgan dysfunction support the diagnosis. [15]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- History and Physical
content: Symptoms may include fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as emesis, diarrhea, and abdominal tenderness. However, fever may be absent in infants, even in inflammation and multiorgan dysfunction. [5] In neonates, symptoms can differ from those of older children due to the developmentally immature immune system. The clinical presentation in neonates predominantly includes gastrointestinal symptoms and poor feeding. [15] Other clinical signs and symptoms include: Bilateral, nonsuppurative rash; conjunctivitis; or mucocutaneous involvement Hypotension, shock, or signs of cardiovascular dysfunction Gastrointestinal involvement, such as emesis, diarrhea, and abdominal tenderness Respiratory distress or pneumonia Neurological impairment, seizures, or signs of meningitis Acute kidney injury Coagulopathy [16]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Evaluation
content: The diagnosis of MIS-C is based on the characteristic clinical presentation, history of exposure to COVID-19, and characteristic laboratory abnormalities. Other diagnoses with similar presentations and evidence of COVID-19 exposure, such as prior maternal SARS-CoV-2 exposure, positive neonatal real-time polymerase chain reaction results, or positive serology testing, should be excluded. The CDC and WHO have published criteria for diagnosing MIS-C in children, but these criteria may not always be accurate for the neonatal population. Currently, there is no universally accepted definition for diagnosing MIS-C in neonates. title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Evaluation
content: Leukocytosis or leukopenia, neutrophilia, anemia, thrombocytopenia Elevated inflammatory markers, including CRP, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6 Elevated cardiac markers such as troponin or B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)/N-terminal pro-BNP (pro-BNP) Coagulopathy, evidenced by prolonged prothrombin time or D-dimer elevation Hypoalbuminemia and hyponatremia Elevated liver and renal function test results Metabolic acidosis and elevated lactate [17]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory findings are variable, especially in the neonatal population. Laboratory evaluation is crucial in suspected cases of MIS-C in neonates to exclude sepsis, quantify inflammation, and detect end-organ dysfunction. Positive neonatal real-time polymerase chain reaction results or positive serology for SARS-CoV-2 are evidence of prior COVID-19 exposure. A history of maternal SARS-CoV-2 exposure should be obtained in infants with negative testing.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Evaluation
content: An electrocardiogram and echocardiogram must be obtained in all neonates with suspected MIS-C to exclude cardiac dysfunction. [16] Infants with elevated troponin or pro-BNP levels or signs of cardiac dysfunction, including hypotension, shock, or need for inotropic support, are at a higher risk for myocardial involvement. [18] Myocardial dysfunction, pericarditis, pericardial effusion, valvulitis, and coronary artery abnormalities have been reported in children and neonates with MIS-C. [19]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Evaluation
content: Chest radiography or computed tomography scan may reveal interstitial pneumonia, pleural effusion, and other abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography should be performed in infants with gastrointestinal symptoms to assess for organomegaly and gallbladder hydrops, and to exclude other possible differential diagnoses. Neuroimaging techniques, such as cranial ultrasonography or magnetic resonance imaging, may be indicated in cases of neurological impairment.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment for neonatal MIS-C is primarily extrapolated from the treatment strategies used in adults and older children. [20] Supportive care remains the cornerstone of treatment, with an emphasis on maintaining adequate cardiorespiratory function, ensuring proper fluid and nutritional support, and regulating body temperature. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and corticosteroids are used to manage the increased inflammatory response and improve symptoms. [16]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Treatment / Management
content: Study results have shown that the combination of IVIG and steroids is more effective than IVIG alone. Inotropic support may be required in cases of cardiovascular dysfunction. Biological agents such as tocilizumab, infliximab, anakinra, and interferons have been used for children and neonates with refractory disease unresponsive to corticosteroids and IVIG. However, data supporting the use of these medications for MIS-C is sparse. [1]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Treatment / Management
content: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are often initiated empirically, as the presentation of MIS-C can mimic neonatal sepsis. Antibiotic treatment should be discontinued once the diagnosis is confirmed and the blood culture results are negative. Thromboprophylaxis is indicated in patients with increased prothrombotic risk factors. [21] [22] The ideal treatment approach should be individualized based on the clinical presentation and disease severity. Further clinical trials are necessary to establish the efficacy and safety of various treatment modalities. Long-term follow-up is necessary to elucidate potential sequelae.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The signs and symptoms of MIS-C can mimic several other conditions. Important differential diagnoses to consider include: Toxic shock syndrome Macrophage activation syndrome Kawasaki disease Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis [23]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Prognosis
content: Short-term outcomes of MIS-C depend on the severity and extent of cardiovascular and respiratory involvement. [24] Reported mortality rates range from 1% to 11%. [25] [26] [27] With timely diagnosis and management, outcomes are generally favorable. Long-term follow-up of infants exposed to COVID-19 antenatally or in the neonatal period is necessary to identify potential sequelae.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Complications
content: The most common complications of MIS-C include respiratory distress and cardiovascular dysfunction. Infants with MIS-C also have an increased risk for prothrombotic coagulopathy and thromboembolic complications, including pulmonary thromboembolism. [28] Case reports have described complications such as deep vein thrombosis, limb ischemia, and intracranial hemorrhage. [29] Additional reported complications include pericardial effusion and acute renal failure. [30]

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Consultations
content: Neonates and infants are usually treated in the neonatal or pediatric intensive care units, and the following specialty consultations are commonly used: Pediatric rheumatology recommends the use of biological medications Pediatric hematology for anticoagulation recommendations Pediatric infectious diseases to evaluate for alternative infectious etiologies Pediatric cardiology in cases with cardiovascular involvement or those requiring inotropic support

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: MIS-C is a disease entity associated with COVID-19, characterized by evolving symptomatology and severity. A deeper understanding of the pathophysiology of MIS-C may lead to more effective treatment approaches. Due to the rapid mutations and contagious nature of the viral infection, COVID-19 infection and its associated sequelae remain a threat, and more effective management strategies are needed. Patients should receive education on the potential complications and long-term outcomes associated with MIS-C.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: MIS-C in neonates, although rare, is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. MIS-C in neonates may present with a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, and early recognition is crucial for improving outcomes. The mainstay of treatment includes supportive management, IVIG, and corticosteroids. More clinical trials are necessary to study the efficacy of various treatment modalities. Long-term follow-up is needed to identify potential sequelae. Study results show that COVID-19 vaccination reduces the risk of MIS-C, with a lower incidence in vaccinated individuals, supporting the protective role of pediatric immunization against postinfectious inflammation. [31] However, the role of maternal vaccination in preventing MIS-C in neonates has yet to be established.

title: Neonatal MIS-C -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The diagnosis and management of MIS-C require an interprofessional team approach. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and is often a diagnosis of exclusion in patients with a known history of COVID-19 exposure. Neonatal intensivists should consider the possibility of MIS-C in neonates with in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. The initial evaluation is often conducted by a neonatologist or pediatric intensivist. Once the diagnosis is established, an interdisciplinary approach involving a pediatric or neonatal intensivist, pediatric cardiology, pediatric infectious disease, pediatric rheumatology, and pediatric hematology is essential for managing the disease and any potential complications. This interprofessional, collaborative team approach is crucial to enhancing patient outcomes. Current evidence on the pathophysiology of neonatal MIS-C is scarce and contradictory. Therefore, well-structured diagnostic criteria and management methods are needed. A deeper understanding of pathophysiology may lead to improved treatment strategies, and data sharing is crucial to formulate optimal treatment approaches.

This interprofessional, collaborative team approach is crucial to enhancing patient outcomes. Current evidence on the pathophysiology of neonatal MIS-C is scarce and contradictory. Therefore, well-structured diagnostic criteria and management methods are needed. A deeper understanding of pathophysiology may lead to improved treatment strategies, and data sharing is crucial to formulate optimal treatment approaches.
